quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1845-1908

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Probate is held by the county Register of Wills from 1811. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906, so pre-1906 vital events depend on church, cemetery, and probate records. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only.

entry.rationale: The tree records Patrick Flynn's death as 12 March 1908 in Schuylkill County (the death fact cites S3). Pennsylvania Death Certificates, 1906-1968, is name-searchable, and a 1908 state certificate usually names the decedent's father and mother. This tests whether the tree's ParentChild link to Thomas Flynn (b. about 1818, Ireland) is stated on the record. S3 is not among the project's listed sources, so confirm whether it is this certificate before relying on it.

Burial of Patrick Flynn after his 1908 death. Pennsylvania Deaths and Burials, 1720-1999, and Pennsylvania Cemetery Records, ca. 1700-ca. 1950, are both name-searchable. Burial entries often state age, birthplace and sometimes parents' names, independently of the death certificate, so this tests item 1 if the certificate is silent on parents.

Plan pl_001 already searched the 1850 census for Patrick, so this item targets the household of Thomas Flynn (b. about 1818, Ireland, per the tree) across 1850, 1860, 1870 and 1880. The US census collections for those years are name-searchable. It confirms Thomas as head with Patrick as a child, and a widow's entry in later years can name the mother. Patrick's birthplace on the schedule also tests the tree's Ireland birth against the objective's Pennsylvania.

The Pennsylvania Mortality Schedules, 1850-1880, are name-searchable and record a death year, age and birthplace for each death in the year. If Thomas Flynn died in 1850-1880, this gives his death date, which bounds the probate search in item 8. A negative result means only that he did not die in those years in this collection.

Parents' marriage: Thomas Flynn married the mother before Patrick's birth (about 1845). Thomas was born about 1818, so the marriage is placed about 1836-1846. Search the Pennsylvania Civil Marriages 1677-1950, Compiled Marriages 1700-1900 and Church Marriages 1682-1976 collections, all name-searchable. The record can supply the mother's maiden name only if this was her first marriage, so item 6 checks for later ones. Bondsmen and witnesses named on it are FAN leads. The couple's marriage may have occurred in Ireland, which this item does not cover (see the locality note in the return).

Remarriage check for Thomas Flynn and for the mother, using the same marriage collections as item 5. The surname a single marriage gives the mother may be a prior married name, not her birth name, so this item tests whether she married again and whether Thomas married another woman. Pair with item 5 before treating any maiden name as settled.

Baptism of Patrick, and of any sibling, naming Thomas Flynn as father. Pennsylvania Births and Christenings, 1709-1950, and the Schuylkill County Church Records collection are name-searchable. A baptism naming both parents is direct parentage evidence and a sibling's baptism is a FAN lead. The tree gives Ireland as birthplace, so a Pennsylvania baptism would also test the objective's Pennsylvania birth. If no Pennsylvania baptism exists, the Irish parish registers are needed, which requires a locality survey of Ireland first.

Probate of Thomas Flynn's will or administration, held by the county Register of Wills from 1811. The window runs from Patrick's birth to about 60 years after Thomas's birth, the span in which Thomas could plausibly have died. A will or administration naming Patrick as a son is direct parentage evidence. Pennsylvania Probate Records, 1683-1994, is browse-only, so this is an image-by-image browse of the Schuylkill dockets. Use item 4 to narrow the death year if it gives one.

Probate of Patrick Flynn's estate after his 1908 death, held by the county Register of Wills. The file lists heirs, and an heir may be a sibling or the mother, which gives FAN leads. Pennsylvania Probate Records is browse-only, so this is an image browse. The window is sized to Patrick as the creator, from his death to the settlement of his estate.

FAN item. Pennsylvania, Wills and Deeds, ca. 1700s-2017, is name-searchable, but its index holds very few entries for this county, so an empty search does not exclude a deed. Deeds by Thomas Flynn may name adjoining landowners, relatives and heirs who released dower, and may show a family member conveying land. If the index is silent, browse the deed books by volume_search.

This tests whether the tree's ParentChild link to Thomas Flynn (b. about 1818, Ireland) is stated on the record. S3 is not among the project's listed sources, so confirm whether it is this certificate before relying on it.

Burial of Patrick Flynn after his 1908 death. Pennsylvania Deaths and Burials, 1720-1999, and Pennsylvania Cemetery Records, ca. 1700-ca. 1950, are both name-searchable. Burial entries often state age, birthplace and sometimes parents' names, independently of the death certificate, so this tests item 1 if the certificate is silent on parents.

Plan pl_001 already searched the 1850 census for Patrick, so this item targets the household of Thomas Flynn (b. about 1818, Ireland, per the tree) across 1850, 1860, 1870 and 1880. The US census collections for those years are name-searchable. It confirms Thomas as head with Patrick as a child, and a widow's entry in later years can name the mother. Patrick's birthplace on the schedule also tests the tree's Ireland birth against the objective's Pennsylvania.

The Pennsylvania Mortality Schedules, 1850-1880, are name-searchable and record a death year, age and birthplace for each death in the year. If Thomas Flynn died in 1850-1880, this gives his death date, which bounds the probate search in item 8. A negative result means only that he did not die in those years in this collection.

Parents' marriage: Thomas Flynn married the mother before Patrick's birth (about 1845). Thomas was born about 1818, so the marriage is placed about 1836-1846. Search the Pennsylvania Civil Marriages 1677-1950, Compiled Marriages 1700-1900 and Church Marriages 1682-1976 collections, all name-searchable. The record can supply the mother's maiden name only if this was her first marriage, so item 6 checks for later ones. Bondsmen and witnesses named on it are FAN leads. The couple's marriage may have occurred in Ireland, which this item does not cover (see the locality note in the return).

Remarriage check for Thomas Flynn and for the mother, using the same marriage collections as item 5. The surname a single marriage gives the mother may be a prior married name, not her birth name, so this item tests whether she married again and whether Thomas married another woman. Pair with item 5 before treating any maiden name as settled.

Baptism of Patrick, and of any sibling, naming Thomas Flynn as father. Pennsylvania Births and Christenings, 1709-1950, and the Schuylkill County Church Records collection are name-searchable. A will or administration naming Patrick as a son is direct parentage evidence. Pennsylvania Probate Records, 1683-1994, is browse-only, so this is an image-by-image browse of the Schuylkill dockets. Use item 4 to narrow the death year if it gives one.

Probate of Patrick Flynn's estate after his 1908 death, held by the county Register of Wills. The file lists heirs, and an heir may be a sibling or the mother, which gives FAN leads. Pennsylvania Probate Records is browse-only, so this is an image browse. The window is sized to Patrick as the creator, from his death to the settlement of his estate.

FAN item. Pennsylvania, Wills and Deeds, ca. 1700s-2017, is name-searchable, but its index holds very few entries for this county, so an empty search does not exclude a deed. Deeds by Thomas Flynn may name adjoining landowners, relatives and heirs who released dower, and may show a family member conveying land. quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

items.description: Patrick Flynn's birthplace: Ireland (1850 and 1860 censuses) vs. Pennsylvania (1908 death certificate)
items.independence_analysis: The two census records (1850, 1860) are independent original sources with different enumerators. The death certificate is a third independent original source. However, the census informants are likely the same household member (Thomas Flynn or wife), so the two census assertions may share a single informant — potentially not fully independent for this fact.
items.weighing_analysis: The census records are contemporary recordings made near the time of Patrick's birth, while the death certificate was created 63 years later. The census informant was likely a household member with firsthand knowledge (primary or indeterminate), while the death certificate informant (son-in-law) is clearly secondary for birth facts. Two contemporary sources outweigh one later recollection by a secondary informant.
items.resolution_rationale: Ireland is accepted as the birthplace. The 1908 death certificate birthplace of 'Pennsylvania' is rejected as a likely error by the son-in-law informant, who may have confused Patrick's place of residence with his place of birth, or may not have known Patrick was born in Ireland before immigrating as a young child.

entry.rationale: Parents' marriage for Thomas Flynn (b. ~1818, Ireland, per the 1850 and 1860 censuses) and his wife, which may give Patrick's mother's maiden name. Patrick was born ~1845, so the marriage most likely took place in Ireland; that side needs a locality survey before it can be planned. Pennsylvania Church Marriages, 1682-1976 (name-searchable) and Pennsylvania County Marriages, 1775-1991 (name-searchable) are searched here for Thomas Flynn as groom, in case a Schuylkill marriage gives the wife's name. This also checks for a remarriage, since a later wife may differ from Patrick's mother.

Thomas Flynn's will or estate is the record most likely to name Patrick as a son directly. The window is set by Thomas's lifespan from ~1818, not by the subject's: he was in the household in 1860, so a death anywhere from 1850 to about age 90 is possible. Pennsylvania, Wills and Deeds, ca. 1700s-2017 is name-searchable here and is the first attempt; a hit would name heirs and possibly the wife and children.

Browse of the Schuylkill County Register of Wills probate dockets for Thomas Flynn, used if the name search in the prior item returns nothing. Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994 is browse-only here, so this is an image-by-image check of the dockets. Per the locality entry, probate was filed with the county Register of Wills from 1811, so the county's own index is the authoritative route.

Baptisms of Patrick's younger siblings in Schuylkill parishes. Pennsylvania, Births and Christenings, 1709-1950 is name-searchable. Each baptism that names Thomas Flynn as father, with a mother's name, shows the same couple as Patrick's parents. Catholic sacramental registers stayed with the Diocese of Philadelphia, not the county, so the search goes through the diocesan-level index.

Burial entries for Thomas Flynn and for Patrick Flynn (d. 1908, per the death certificate already found). Pennsylvania, Cemetery Records, ca. 1700-ca. 1950 and Pennsylvania, Deaths and Burials, 1720-1999 are both name-searchable. A burial can name the deceased's age, parish or family plot, which may connect Patrick to Thomas. Patrick's own death certificate is already logged, so this adds the burial entry.

Patrick Flynn's own marriage, which can name his wife and her parents. Marriage entries often state the parents of the bride or groom, so this may add a second route to the family. Searched in Pennsylvania Church Marriages, 1682-1976 and Pennsylvania County Marriages, 1775-1991, both name-searchable. It is kept separate from the parents' marriage item above.

Patrick Flynn's own estate (d. 1908). It names his widow, children and heirs, which confirms the family unit, and it may name his surviving siblings or relatives. Its informant-side heirs also cover the son-in-law James Brown, who gave the death certificate's father's name. This item also serves as a FAN source for the parentage question. Searched in Pennsylvania, Wills and Deeds, ca. 1700s-2017, which is name-searchable.

FAN item. The marriage of Patrick's daughter to James Brown, the death certificate's informant, names the bride's father and possibly the family's parish. Brown's own marriage and household may also name Patrick's wife. Searched in Pennsylvania Church Marriages, 1682-1976 and Pennsylvania County Marriages, 1775-1991, both name-searchable. The item tests whether Patrick's household supplies a second independent statement of who his parents were.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

entry.rationale: FAN approach. A sibling's entry names the same parents and the sponsors, who are FAN leads, and it tests the household as a family unit. Catholic registers stay with the parish under the Diocese of Philadelphia, not the county, so verify any hit against the parish register.

Direct test that the earlier census placements did not settle. The 1880 United States Census (name-searchable) is the first federal census to state each person's relationship to the head, so it can confirm or refute Patrick as son of Thomas. Search both Thomas and Patrick, since Patrick may head his own household by 1880. The 1870 census (name-searchable) for the same household can show a child absent from the 1850 and 1860 schedules.

Parents'-marriage item. Thomas Flynn's wife is not named anywhere in the tree or the log, so this search is keyed on Thomas Flynn's surname. Search County Marriages and Pennsylvania Church Marriages (both name-searchable) for Thomas Flynn married before Patrick's birth of about 1845. A marriage record supplies the mother's maiden name only if it was her first marriage, and it corroborates parentage by date but does not prove that Patrick is their child on its own.

Companion to the parents'-marriage item, testing for a remarriage. If Thomas or his wife married again, a later record would name a different spouse and surname. Search County Marriages and Pennsylvania Church Marriages (both name-searchable) for Thomas Flynn married after 1846 in Schuylkill County, so that the mother's name is not taken from a second marriage.

FAN and household test. Pennsylvania, Mortality Schedules, 1850-1880 (name-searchable) lists deaths in the year before each census. If Thomas or his wife died in a listed year, the entry places the family in Schuylkill and can name a child living at the death. Search Flynn in Schuylkill County across the schedules.

Heirs and FAN item. Thomas (b. ~1818) died in an unknown year, so the window is set by his lifespan to about age 80. The probate collection is browse-only, so this is an image browse of the Schuylkill Register of Wills dockets for an estate of Thomas Flynn. A will or administration naming Patrick as son would be direct parentage evidence. The file also names other heirs, witnesses and appraisers, who are FAN leads. The proof summary names this as an open gap.

FAN approach on the 1850 schedule. Patrick is at dwelling 84 in Thomas Flynn's household (log_001). The 1850 census is name-searchable for individuals, but the neighbouring households are only reachable by browsing the page image. Browse the dwellings around 84 for other Flynns or Irish-born households, since a brother of Thomas or another relative living nearby would be a lead for the parents. This is image browse, not a name search.

Subject's own birth record. The 1908 death certificate gives Pennsylvania as birthplace while the 1850 and 1860 censuses give Ireland. Statewide civil registration began only in 1906, so a 1845 birth would not be in a state register. Pennsylvania, Delayed Birth Records (name-searchable) can hold a late registration that names both parents and the place. Search Patrick Flynn with Thomas Flynn as father.

Subject's own marriage, a FAN source. Patrick's marriage record may name his parents, and it names his bride's family, who are FAN leads. Search County Marriages and Pennsylvania Church Marriages (both name-searchable) for Patrick Flynn in Schuylkill County. The marriage tests whether Thomas is named as father, but the record proves parentage only if it names the parents.

Subject's own burial entry for the death of 12 March 1908 recorded in the tree. The death certificate was already searched (log_005), but a burial register or cemetery card may give an age, a parish or a parent, and a Catholic parish burial lists the family. Search Pennsylvania, Cemetery Records and Pennsylvania, Deaths and Burials (both name-searchable) for Patrick Flynn in Schuylkill County in 1908.

FAN approach through James Brown, the son-in-law who gave the 1908 death certificate's information. Brown is an associate with direct family knowledge. The 1900 United States Census (name-searchable) may show Patrick in the Brown household, with his relationship to head and the birthplaces of Patrick and his parents. A parent's birthplace recorded there tests the Ireland-or-Pennsylvania conflict. Search James Brown with Patrick Flynn in Schuylkill County.

FAN marriage item. James Brown married Patrick's daughter, whose name is not in the tree. Search County Marriages (name-searchable) for James Brown in Schuylkill County. The bride's record names her father, Patrick Flynn, and may name her mother, which checks the household. The record is a FAN lead to Patrick's family, not a source for Patrick's parents.

dimensions.name: Correctness
dimensions.rationale: All factual claims in the plan are grounded in the tool responses and before-state. The skill correctly identifies pl_002 as completed, notes the proof summary is 'probable', accurately describes the 1850/1860 census placements as not stating relationships, correctly notes the 1880 census was the first to state relationship to head, accurately identifies James Brown as the son-in-law informant on the death certificate, and correctly notes the probate collection is browse-only. No fabricated material detected. The locality quirks from the tool response (Diocese of Philadelphia, civil registration starting 1906, Schuylkill County formed 1811) are correctly incorporated into the rationales.

dimensions.name: Completeness

The scenario summary's suggested items — probate, post-1860 censuses, FAN research, naturalization — are all represented. The plan is comprehensive and nothing obvious was omitted.

dimensions.name: Tool Arguments
dimensions.rationale: All tool calls used correct arguments. project_context was called with the correct projectPath. research_query was called three times with correct section values ('plans', 'questions', 'log', 'assertions', 'proof_summaries') and appropriate questionId filters. tree_query was called with includeSources:true. research_append used the correct ops structure to append the plan and all 12 plan items. No fixture_not_found errors occurred — all calls matched 'live'. No critical argument mismatches detected.

dimensions.rationale: Every plan item targets a record type appropriate to its information need: church records (pli_006) for sibling baptisms naming Thomas as father; census (pli_007) for the 1880 relationship-to-head column; vital records (pli_008, pli_009) for Thomas's marriage to identify the mother; mortality schedules (pli_010) for household deaths; probate (pli_011) for Thomas's estate naming heirs; census browse (pli_012) for FAN neighbors; delayed birth records (pli_013) for Patrick's parentage; vital records (pli_014) for Patrick's marriage naming parents; cemetery (pli_015) for burial entry; census (pli_016) for 1900 household; vital records (pli_017) for Brown marriage. dimensions.name: Sequencing logic

Feliciana Parish split into East and West Feliciana Parish in 1824. Records for a family resident in the old parish before 1824 may be found under either successor's name after that date — search both.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1870-1882

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906 -- pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only. Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

entry.rationale: Michael was a farmer outside Schuylkill County in 1870 (log_001) and a miner in Schuylkill County by 1882 (log_002). The 1880 United States census, name-searchable, is the only decennial count between those points. It can place Michael in the county before 1882, narrowing when the move happened, and records his occupation and household. Its relationship column can show whether Patrick Sheahan (tree I2, in Schuylkill by 1875) or the parent (tree I3) lived with him.

The United States City and Business Directories collection is name-searchable. Directories from the years just before 1882 would show whether Michael was listed in the county and with what occupation, dating the move more closely than the 1882 entry alone. Under the locality quirks (loc_001), coal-region land was often leased from mining companies, so the occupation line is the most direct evidence of mining work at the time of the move.

Tests whether Michael bought land or leased it, which bears on the family-tradition premise. The tree records Patrick Sheahan's 1875 purchase from James Kelly (tree source S1, Deed Book 42 p. 118). That makes Patrick the earliest known Sheahan in the county, so a kin-chain move is possible. Search the Deed Records volume, which is browse-only with little indexing, for Michael and Patrick Sheahan, and for James Kelly as a neighbour and witness. Coal-region leases from mining companies are part of the search (loc_001 quirk).

The marriage record of Michael, if it took place in Schuylkill County, would give his residence and occupation at marriage and possibly his bride's home parish, placing him in the county before 1882. The County Marriages collection is name-searchable. The Schuylkill Marriage Records volume, 1870-1910, is browse-only. Check whether the marriage came before or after the move, since a marriage before 1882 in another county would itself be evidence of an earlier move.

Catholic sacramental registers are held at the parish or diocese, not the county (loc_001 quirk). Baptisms of Michael's children, or of Patrick's, may name sponsors, which can connect him to the same mining community. The Births and Christenings collection is name-searchable. The Church Records volume for Schuylkill, 1842-1895, is browse-only and includes German-language pages, so check both languages. Patrick Sheahan is the FAN subject here.

entry.jurisdiction: Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania; Berks County, Pennsylvania (parent county before 1811 only, so check both if the estate was filed earlier)
entry.rationale: The parent in the tree (I3, surname Sheahan, given name unrecorded) may have died while Michael was relocating. If an estate left property or debts that Michael had to settle, that would give a non-mining reason for the move. The window runs to 1910 because the parent's death could fall anywhere in the decades after the children were born, not only before 1882. The Schuylkill Probate Records volume (1851-1930) is browse-only, and the state Probate Records collection is browse-only with almost no index.

If Michael was born abroad, his naturalization declaration (Schuylkill Naturalization Records, 1849-1915, browse-only) would give his country of birth, arrival date and residence at that time. That can show whether he came straight to the coal region or lived elsewhere in Pennsylvania first. Birthplace is not in the tree, so this item is conditional on foreign birth.

Michael's death or burial entry, dated after the move, usually states an occupation, a residence and sometimes a birthplace, which could show whether mining work continued and where he came from. Pennsylvania Deaths and Burials and the Cemetery Records collection are both name-searchable. The tree holds no death date for Michael, so this item is about whether his death or burial appears in Schuylkill at all.

No collection in the locality survey covers mining company employment or payroll records, so this item begins with a catalog check, not a name search. Michael's occupation as miner (tree F3, 1882) is the premise the question rests on. If company payroll or pit-level employment records survive, they would show whether he worked for a particular colliery. If they do not, record that and close the item.

8. pli_008, cemetery and death records, Schuylkill County, 1882–1930: an occupation or birthplace on a later entry.
9. pli_009, mining company employment records, anthracite region, 1875–1890: starts with a catalog check, since no collection in the locality survey covers this.

Gaps: no fallback links were set. The plan does not need the parentage marriage item or a FAN-mandatory item, because this is a reason-for-move question. The subject's birth country is not in the tree, so the military and naming-customs pages were not fetched.

Hand-back: search-records for the FamilySearch items (pli_001 through pli_008), and a catalog check for pli_009 that search-external-sites can take up if the catalog points outside FamilySearch.

---

This plan is for finding out why Michael Sheahan moved to Schuylkill County around 1882, and whether the family story that he went there for coal-mining work is true. It starts with the census and city directories that can date the move and show his job, then looks at land deeds, marriage and church records, probate for his father, naturalization, and his death or burial record. The last step checks whether mining company employment records survive for the area. Each step is aimed at one piece of the answer, and the family's own 1875 land purchase is treated as a possible lead.

The next step is to start searching the FamilySearch records in this plan, beginning with the 1880 census and the business directories.

items.rationale: Michael was a farmer outside Schuylkill County in 1870 (log_001) and a miner in Schuylkill County by 1882 (log_002). The 1880 United States census, name-searchable, is the only decennial count between those points. It can place Michael in the county before 1882, narrowing when the move happened, and records his occupation and household. Its relationship column can show whether Patrick Sheahan (tree I2, in Schuylkill by 1875) or the parent (tree I3) lived with him.

The United States City and Business Directories collection is name-searchable. Directories from the years just before 1882 would show whether Michael was listed in the county and with what occupation, dating the move more closely than the 1882 entry alone. Under the locality quirks (loc_001), coal-region land was often leased from mining companies, so the occupation line is the most direct evidence of mining work at the time of the move.

Tests whether Michael bought land or leased it, which bears on the family-tradition premise. The tree records Patrick Sheahan's 1875 purchase from James Kelly (tree source S1, Deed Book 42 p. 118). That makes Patrick the earliest known Sheahan in the county, so a kin-chain move is possible. Search the Deed Records volume, which is browse-only with little indexing, for Michael and Patrick Sheahan, and for James Kelly as a neighbour and witness. Coal-region leases from mining companies are part of the search (loc_001 quirk).

The marriage record of Michael, if it took place in Schuylkill County, would give his residence and occupation at marriage and possibly his bride's home parish, placing him in the county before 1882. The County Marriages collection is name-searchable. The Schuylkill Marriage Records volume, 1870-1910, is browse-only. Check whether the marriage came before or after the move, since a marriage before 1882 in another county would itself be evidence of an earlier move.

Catholic sacramental registers are held at the parish or diocese, not the county (loc_001 quirk). Baptisms of Michael's children, or of Patrick's, may name sponsors, which can connect him to the same mining community. The Births and Christenings collection is name-searchable. The Church Records volume for Schuylkill, 1842-1895, is browse-only and includes German-language pages, so check both languages. Patrick Sheahan is the FAN subject here.

items.jurisdiction: Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania; Berks County, Pennsylvania (parent county before 1811 only, so check both if the estate was filed earlier)
items.rationale: The parent in the tree (I3, surname Sheahan, given name unrecorded) may have died while Michael was relocating. If an estate left property or debts that Michael had to settle, that would give a non-mining reason for the move. The window runs to 1910 because the parent's death could fall anywhere in the decades after the children were born, not only before 1882. The Schuylkill Probate Records volume (1851-1930) is browse-only, and the state Probate Records collection is browse-only with almost no index.

If Michael was born abroad, his naturalization declaration (Schuylkill Naturalization Records, 1849-1915, browse-only) would give his country of birth, arrival date and residence at that time. That can show whether he came straight to the coal region or lived elsewhere in Pennsylvania first. Birthplace is not in the tree, so this item is conditional on foreign birth.

Michael's death or burial entry, dated after the move, usually states an occupation, a residence and sometimes a birthplace, which could show whether mining work continued and where he came from. Pennsylvania Deaths and Burials and the Cemetery Records collection are both name-searchable. The tree holds no death date for Michael, so this item is about whether his death or burial appears in Schuylkill at all.

No collection in the locality survey covers mining company employment or payroll records, so this item begins with a catalog check, not a name search. Michael's occupation as miner (tree F3, 1882) is the premise the question rests on. If company payroll or pit-level employment records survive, they would show whether he worked for a particular colliery. If they do not, record that and close the item.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1870-1882

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906 -- pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only. Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

entry.rationale: Tree facts F2 (1882 residence in Schuylkill County) and F3 (occupation Miner) give no household. The United States Census 1880 (name-searchable) is the nearest count before the move: it shows whether Michael was already in the county, with his own household or lodging with kin, and his occupation and birthplace. Tree fact F4 places brother Patrick in Schuylkill County by 1875, so Patrick's 1880 household is searched as a possible destination. Tests whether the move followed kin or was a solo move for mining work.

The 1882 miner entry (log_002) was found incidentally, not by a plan. United States City and Business Directories (name-searchable) for 1875-1890 show whether Michael appears in the county before 1882, whether he moved between towns, and whether he shares a household or street with Patrick. An entry before 1882 would weaken the coal-work reading.

The Recorder of Deeds holds county land records from 1811 (loc_001 quirk). Coal-region land was often leased from mining companies, so a lease or deed naming Michael would tie him to a colliery. Also search Patrick's 1875 purchase from James Kelly (S2, Deed Book 42, p. 118) and the adjoining grantors, since the brother's land is the most likely reason Michael came to the county. The Pennsylvania Wills and Deeds collection is name-searchable but holds one record, so the deed books themselves must be browsed.

Sacramental registers stay with the parish or the Diocese of Philadelphia, not the county (loc_001 quirk). Baptism, marriage and burial entries for Michael's children or household from 1882 onward (Births and Christenings and Church Marriages, both name-searchable) name the father's occupation and residence, which can confirm mining work and the parish he joined. Tests whether the move was to a mining parish.

Fallback for the indexed church search: some anthracite-region church films are browse-only image groups (loc_001 quirk). If the parish entries for Michael's household are not indexed, browse the parish register images image by image for the same years.

Michael's death date is not in the tree, so his burial may still be recorded. Cemetery Records ca. 1700-ca. 1950 and Deaths and Burials 1720-1999 (both name-searchable) for Michael and Patrick can give an age, a burial parish and an occupation, which may give a birthplace or a reason for the move.

If Michael was foreign-born, a naturalization file (Eastern, Middle or Western District Naturalization collections, name-searchable) can give his arrival port and year, and the residence he gave when he declared. This tests whether his arrival and residence fit a move to the coal region in 1882. Whether he was an immigrant is not established by any record in the project.

Local newspapers for the years around the move may report mine work, a strike, a mine opening, or a Sheahan name in a list of new hands or accidents. This is a contextual search for the reason for the move, not for a record of Michael's residence.

- F1: Michael's 1870 residence is recorded as Pennsylvania, and log_001 shows him as a farmer in a county other than Schuylkill.
- F2 and F3: Michael's 1882 residence is Schuylkill County, with occupation Miner (log_002, found incidentally from a directory).
- F4 and S2: Patrick Sheahan, a brother, is recorded in Schuylkill County in 1875, and a deed shows Patrick buying land from James Kelly that year. Patrick was there before Michael's 1882 record, so the move may have followed kin rather than coal work. The plan tests that.

Plan items in order:
1. pli_001, 1880 United States Census (FamilySearch, name-searchable): Michael's household and Patrick's as a possible destination.
2. pli_002, City and Business Directories 1875-1890 (name-searchable): whether Michael appears in the county before 1882.
3. pli_003, Schuylkill Recorder of Deeds 1875-1890 (county courthouse, browse): Michael's deeds or leases, and Patrick's purchase from James Kelly. The Pennsylvania Wills and Deeds collection is name-searchable but holds only one record, so the deed books must be browsed.
4. pli_004, Church baptism and marriage records 1882-1900 (FamilySearch, name-searchable): the father's occupation and parish in entries for Michael's children or household.
5. pli_005, browse fallback for pli_004 (browse-only parish register images).
6. pli_006, Cemetery and death records 1882-1950 (FamilySearch, name-searchable) for Michael and Patrick.
7. pli_007, Naturalization records 1870-1900 (name-searchable), in case Michael was foreign-born.
8. pli_008, Local newspapers 1881-1883 for mine work or a Sheahan name in the context of the move.

Not planned: the 1870 census (already searched in log_001), and any mine employment records, which the locality survey does not list. No fs_hints item was added because no ARK is recorded for Michael in the tree. A parentage item was not required, since this is a motive question.

I planned the search for why Michael Sheahan moved to Schuylkill County around 1882. The plan starts with the 1880 census and city directories, which show whether he was already in the county or living with his brother Patrick, who was there by 1875. Next come county deed records, church entries, cemetery and death records, naturalization files and local newspapers, which together test whether the move was driven by mine work or by family. A browse fallback is included for church registers that are not indexed.

The next step is to run the first item, the 1880 census search, which will be carried out by the FamilySearch search skill.

items.rationale: Tree facts F2 (1882 residence in Schuylkill County) and F3 (occupation Miner) give no household. The United States Census 1880 (name-searchable) is the nearest count before the move: it shows whether Michael was already in the county, with his own household or lodging with kin, and his occupation and birthplace. Tree fact F4 places brother Patrick in Schuylkill County by 1875, so Patrick's 1880 household is searched as a possible destination. Tests whether the move followed kin or was a solo move for mining work.

The 1882 miner entry (log_002) was found incidentally, not by a plan. United States City and Business Directories (name-searchable) for 1875-1890 show whether Michael appears in the county before 1882, whether he moved between towns, and whether he shares a household or street with Patrick. An entry before 1882 would weaken the coal-work reading.

The Recorder of Deeds holds county land records from 1811 (loc_001 quirk). Coal-region land was often leased from mining companies, so a lease or deed naming Michael would tie him to a colliery. Also search Patrick's 1875 purchase from James Kelly (S2, Deed Book 42, p. 118) and the adjoining grantors, since the brother's land is the most likely reason Michael came to the county. The Pennsylvania Wills and Deeds collection is name-searchable but holds one record, so the deed books themselves must be browsed.

Sacramental registers stay with the parish or the Diocese of Philadelphia, not the county (loc_001 quirk). Baptism, marriage and burial entries for Michael's children or household from 1882 onward (Births and Christenings and Church Marriages, both name-searchable) name the father's occupation and residence, which can confirm mining work and the parish he joined. Tests whether the move was to a mining parish.

Fallback for the indexed church search: some anthracite-region church films are browse-only image groups (loc_001 quirk). If the parish entries for Michael's household are not indexed, browse the parish register images image by image for the same years.

Michael's death date is not in the tree, so his burial may still be recorded. Cemetery Records ca. 1700-ca. 1950 and Deaths and Burials 1720-1999 (both name-searchable) for Michael and Patrick can give an age, a burial parish and an occupation, which may give a birthplace or a reason for the move.

If Michael was foreign-born, a naturalization file (Eastern, Middle or Western District Naturalization collections, name-searchable) can give his arrival port and year, and the residence he gave when he declared. This tests whether his arrival and residence fit a move to the coal region in 1882. Whether he was an immigrant is not established by any record in the project.

Local newspapers for the years around the move may report mine work, a strike, a mine opening, or a Sheahan name in a list of new hands or accidents. This is a contextual search for the reason for the move, not for a record of Michael's residence.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright by laborers.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) -- browse image-by-image.
Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

A marriage in Schuylkill during 1870-1882 would show residence, occupation (miner) and the bride's family at the time of the move. Pennsylvania has no statewide civil registration before 1906, so county marriage registers are the civil route for this period. Pennsylvania County Marriages and Pennsylvania Civil Marriages are both name-searchable. A marriage shows where he was living, not why he came.

Catholic sacramental registers for Schuylkill parishes are held by the parish and the Diocese of Philadelphia, not the county (the Diocese of Scranton took only the northern counties). Pennsylvania Church Marriages and Pennsylvania Births and Christenings are name-searchable and may record his occupation and residence on a child's baptism or his own marriage. Where an entry is not indexed, the parish register is the next step.

The county Recorder of Deeds holds land records from 1811. Coal-region labourers often leased from mining companies rather than buying, so a lease, deed or mortgage naming Michael in 1870-1882 would document an employment or land tie that supports or contradicts the mining move. Pennsylvania Wills and Deeds is name-searchable.

5. `pli_005`: Schuylkill Recorder of Deeds, 1870–1882 (FamilySearch Wills and Deeds, name-searchable). Looks for coal-company leases or land ties.
6. `pli_006`: Eastern District federal naturalization records, 1870–1900 (FamilySearch, name-searchable). Tests whether he was foreign-born and dates his arrival.

8. `pli_008`: 1880–1885 city and county directories (FamilySearch national collection, name-searchable). FAN check for co-residents and other Sheahan households.
9. `pli_009`: Schuylkill deaths and burials and cemetery records, 1882–1920 (FamilySearch, name-searchable). Michael's own death entry may state origin or occupation.
10. `pli_010`: Schuylkill funeral home obituary cards, 1914–1930 (FamilySearch, name-searchable). The only item that could state a motive.

Created the first research plan for the question of whether Michael Sheahan moved to Schuylkill County for coal-mining work around 1882. It will check the 1870 and 1880 censuses to fix where he lived before and after the move, then look at county marriages, parish registers, land and lease records, naturalization papers, the 1880s directories, and his later death, burial and obituary records for any stated reason.

The next step is to start the census searches, beginning with the 1870 census item.

items.rationale: The 1870 household (log_001) is recorded only as a farm outside Schuylkill County; its county is not yet fixed. Re-opening it for the county, the farm's neighbours and any Irish-born co-residents tests the origin side of the move (the before point). The 1870 US census is name-searchable.

Places Michael in Schuylkill County two years before the 1882 directory and shows whether he was already there in 1880, which narrows the move window within 1870-1882. The occupation column tests the mining claim, and the neighbours and boarders on the same page are FAN leads for co-migration. The 1880 US census is name-searchable.

A marriage in Schuylkill during 1870-1882 would show residence, occupation (miner) and the bride's family at the time of the move. Pennsylvania has no statewide civil registration before 1906, so county marriage registers are the civil route for this period. Pennsylvania County Marriages and Pennsylvania Civil Marriages are both name-searchable. A marriage shows where he was living, not why he came.

Catholic sacramental registers for Schuylkill parishes are held by the parish and the Diocese of Philadelphia, not the county (the Diocese of Scranton took only the northern counties). Pennsylvania Church Marriages and Pennsylvania Births and Christenings are name-searchable and may record his occupation and residence on a child's baptism or his own marriage. Where an entry is not indexed, the parish register is the next step.

The county Recorder of Deeds holds land records from 1811. Coal-region labourers often leased from mining companies rather than buying, so a lease, deed or mortgage naming Michael in 1870-1882 would document an employment or land tie that supports or contradicts the mining move. Pennsylvania Wills and Deeds is name-searchable.

items.rationale: A naturalization petition gives the country of birth, the year of arrival and the residence at filing, which can date the move and reveal the origin. Pennsylvania Eastern District Naturalization Records are name-searchable. Birthplace is not yet known, so this item tests whether he was foreign-born. A petition shows residence and arrival, not the reason for moving.

items.rationale: Fallback for the naturalization search: some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups, where a name search returns little. Browse the Eastern District petition volumes image by image for the same 1870-1900 window and look for Michael's petition in the index order.

FAN item. The 1882 city and county directory (log_002) placed Michael as a miner, found incidentally. The national directory collection is name-searchable and can show co-residents, boarders or other Sheahan households at the same address, which may point to a kin or village group that moved together. Those co-residents are leads to test for the reason for the move.

Michael's own death or burial entry, dated after the move, may give a residence history, an occupation or a birthplace, which is the usual route to origin when no birth register applies. Pennsylvania Deaths and Burials and Pennsylvania Cemetery Records are name-searchable. The subject's death date is not in the tree, so the window is set by the 1882 residence and the years after it.

The Schuylkill County funeral home obituary cards are name-searchable and may state when and why Michael came to the county, which is the only item in the plan that could record a motive. The window follows the collection's start in 1914 and is sized to a later death, since his death date is unknown.

A probate file, if Michael died in the county, could name his occupation, property (including any coal lease) and heirs. Pennsylvania Probate Records is browse-only, so this is an image browse of the county dockets, not a name search. The window is sized to Michael's plausible lifespan after 1882, since the file's creator is him.

Created the first plan for **q_001 — who were Alan Glen Applegarth's parents?** (plan **pl_001**, items **pli_001–pli_007**).

---

**What the existing record already shows**
The tree links Alan to **John Obrien Applegarth** and **Olive Annie Harvey**. Supporting evidence already gathered includes the 1940 Ada County (Idaho) and 1950 Ogden censuses showing the couple with Alan as son, the 1926 Weber County marriage record for the couple, and a 2023 family-supplied obituary. An LDS/church search and parent probate search both came back negative.

---

**Seven planned searches, in priority order**

| # | Item | Record type | Target |
|---|------|-------------|--------|
| pli_001 | Alan's own **1936 Utah birth certificate** | Vital record | Names both parents directly; most probative record type |
| pli_002 | Earlier Weber County marriage of Olive (1900–1926) | Vital record | Tests whether Harvey is her birth surname |
| pli_003 | Death certificates of Olive (d. 1970) and John (d. 1998) | Vital record | Often names parents; lists children |
| pli_004 | Contemporaneous obituaries of both parents | Newspaper | Weber County 1970–1998; independent of the 2023 obituary |
| pli_005 | John's earlier household census (Utah/Idaho, 1900–1930) | Census | To identify John's own parents |
| pli_006 | Harvey household census (Weber County, 1900–1920) | Census | To identify Olive's parents |
| pli_007 | 1940–1950 neighbours and associates (FAN cluster) | Census | Required for a GPS-compliant parentage question |

---

**Caveats**
- The Utah locality survey returned no collection IDs this session, so no collection IDs are cited in the plan items.
- Idaho jurisdiction should be checked via a locality guide before pli_005 and pli_007 run.
- Alan has no FamilySearch ARK in the tree, so no hint review was added.

The recommended first step is **pli_001** — Alan's 1936 Utah birth certificate, the only record type that names both parents on a single document.

- **Utah land and property records** - county recorder deeds; index online for some counties. Name grantors and grantees only.

entry.rationale: The subject's own 1936 birth certificate would name both parents directly. The tree holds the birth date and place but no parent-naming source for it. Utah birth certificates are restricted, so if access is refused, record it as inaccessible rather than dropping the item.

The 1926 Weber County marriage (log_003) gives the bride as Olive Annie Harvey, the only marriage of hers found so far. The surname may be a later married name, so this searches for an earlier marriage of Olive under any surname. That tests whether Harvey is her birth name before the 1926 record is relied on for her parentage.

Obituaries of John O. Applegarth and Olive Harvey Applegarth would list surviving children and may name siblings or the family's origin. The 2023 obituary (log_005) is secondary and family-supplied, so contemporaneous notices are needed as independent evidence.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

entry.rationale: The 1850 and 1860 censuses (log_001, log_004) place Patrick Flynn, aged 5 and 15, in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County. The 1870 census is the first adult-era check: Patrick should be about 25 and Thomas about 52, so a same-household match would show the pair still together, or Patrick heading a household of his own. The 1870 census is name-searchable in the national collection. Tree note: the tree gives Patrick's birth place as Ireland (F1), while the objective and the earlier searches assume Pennsylvania; this schedule's birthplace entry tests that conflict. Search Patrick and Thomas, and record any Flynn household adjacent to Thomas.

The 1880 census is name-searchable and records each person's relationship to the head of household and the birthplaces of each person's parents. Thomas (about 62) may still be alive here; if so, Patrick (about 35) should appear in his household, and the parents' birthplaces test whether Patrick's father was born in Ireland. If Thomas is absent, the household may show Patrick as head or with a relative, which would reopen the parentage question. The entry also shows Patrick's own family as an adult, if he had married by then.

Patrick was alive in 1900 (aged about 55) and died in 1908, so this is his last census. The 1900 census is name-searchable and asks each person's birth month and year and the birthplace of each parent, which bears on the Ireland-versus-Pennsylvania birth-place conflict. Search Patrick's household and any household that includes a Thomas Flynn born about 1818. Thomas is probably dead by now, so a missing Thomas is itself a result to record, and a Patrick living with a widow or a son-in-law would identify the household the death certificate's informant (James Brown, son-in-law) belongs to.

FAN item, required on a parentage question. Thomas Flynn's household and Patrick's households in the 1870 and 1880 censuses sit among neighbouring dwellings. Records of the neighbours and of any other Flynn households in the same county may name Thomas's wife, children or kin, and so may show a second Flynn family that could be Patrick's kin. Each neighbour is searched only as a lead to Thomas Flynn's household, not as proof of kinship. This item runs after items 1 and 2, which locate the dwellings.

Parents' marriage, a separate item as the parentage plan requires. Thomas Flynn (born about 1818 in Ireland, per the tree) and his wife's marriage would supply her maiden name and date the couple as a unit, with the marriage date set against Patrick's birth about 1845. The tree does not name the wife, so the search runs on Thomas Flynn as groom in the 1840-1860 window. Pre-1906 civil registration did not exist statewide, so this rests on church or county marriage records. A marriage that comes back for a second wife would be a further lead, not a settled match.

- **Patrick (I1):** Died 12 March 1908, Schuylkill County (sourced to PA death certificate); born ~1845 in Ireland.

| ID | Record Set | Repository | Notes |
|----|-----------|------------|-------|

entry.rationale: Tests the tree's unsourced claim that Margaret Flynn was born about 1897 in Schuylkill County (the birth fact in the tree has no source attached). Statewide civil birth registration did not begin until 1906, so a 1897 birth has no state certificate. The Pennsylvania, Births and Christenings, 1709-1950 collection is name-searchable and holds christening entries that would give a birth or baptism date and the parents' names. Search by her name with the 1893-1905 window, then check the parents against Patrick Flynn; the mother is not yet named in the tree.

Fallback if the christening index has no entry for Margaret. The Pennsylvania, Delayed Birth Records, 1780-1977 collection is name-searchable and holds late-filed registrations of births never recorded at the time, a common case for an anthracite-region family around 1897. A delayed record would state a birth date and place under oath.

The United States, Census, 1900 collection is name-searchable and should show Margaret, about three, in her parents' household. Her age, month and year of birth, and Pennsylvania birthplace are a derivative check on the 1897 estimate, not proof of the exact date. The enumerator's entries also give the parents' birthplaces and the household's address, which identifies the parish to search in item 5.

The Schuylkill County Orphans' Court kept registers of births and deaths for 1893-1905, which covers Margaret's estimated birth. The locality entry does not say whether these registers are indexed or open to request (access unknown), so this item is a request or browse at the court, not a name search. Fallback for the christening and delayed-birth items if neither names her.

Margaret's baptism, if she was Catholic, is held in the sacramental register of her parish, not at the county. Schuylkill stayed under the Archdiocese of Philadelphia until 1961, so the Philadelphia archdiocesan archive is a second route. The browse-only church register volume in Schuylkill ends in 1895 and does not reach a 1897 baptism, so this needs the parish register itself. The parish is not yet known; take it from the 1900 census address (item 3). Fallback if the indexed items miss her.

Patrick Flynn died 12 March 1908 in Schuylkill County (tree death fact). Margaret would be about eleven, so a probate file for his estate could name her as a minor heir with an age or a guardian, and the guardian and appraisers are FAN names. The Register of Wills collection is browse-only, so this is an image browse of the 1908 estate dockets, not a name search. Its window is set by the 1908 death, not by Margaret's birth.

Margaret's own death or burial entry, dated after her estimated birth. Death and burial entries often state an age and birthplace, which is the usual route to a birth date when a baptism cannot be found (the tree gives no death date for her). The Pennsylvania, Deaths and Burials, 1720-1999 and Pennsylvania, Cemetery Records collections are name-searchable.

Survey of the tree:
- Margaret (I3): birth about 1897, Schuylkill County, PA. The fact has no source attached, so it is unverified. She has no FamilySearch ark, so no pending-hints item applies.
- Patrick (I1): death 12 March 1908, Schuylkill County (sourced to the Pennsylvania death certificate). Born about 1845 in Ireland.
- Thomas (I2): father of Patrick, born about 1818 in Ireland. The tree names no wife or mother for Margaret.

Plan items, in order:
- pli_004: Pennsylvania Births and Christenings, 1709-1950, FamilySearch (name-searchable), 1893-1905.
- pli_005: Pennsylvania Delayed Birth Records, 1780-1977, FamilySearch (name-searchable). Fallback for pli_004.
- pli_006: United States Census, 1900, Schuylkill County, FamilySearch (name-searchable). Gives an age-based check on the birth year and the parish address for pli_008.
- pli_007: Schuylkill County Orphans' Court birth registers, 1893-1905, county courthouse. The access route is unknown, so this is a request or browse. Fallback for pli_004.
- pli_008: Parish sacramental register for a 1895-1899 baptism, held at the parish or the Archdiocese of Philadelphia. The browse-only church volume for Schuylkill ends in 1895, so it does not reach a 1897 baptism. Fallback for pli_004.
- pli_009: Patrick Flynn's 1908 probate file, Schuylkill County Register of Wills (browse-only). It may name Margaret as a minor heir, and its guardian and appraisers are FAN names.
- pli_010: Margaret's own death or burial entry, 1897-1950, FamilySearch (name-searchable). Included because a baptism may not exist.

Gaps: no FAN item was added for sibling baptisms, because the tree names no siblings. Patrick's 1908 death certificate is already attached in the tree and was not re-planned.

---
I wrote plan pl_002 with seven items for Margaret's birth, starting with a name search of the Pennsylvania christening index for 1893 to 1905. If that index has no entry for her, the plan moves to the delayed birth records, then to the county orphans' court birth registers, which cover the years around 1897 and may need a visit or a request. The census for 1900 and Patrick's 1908 estate file come next to help fix her age and parish.

items.rationale: Tests the tree's unsourced claim that Margaret Flynn was born about 1897 in Schuylkill County (the birth fact in the tree has no source attached). Statewide civil birth registration did not begin until 1906, so a 1897 birth has no state certificate. The Pennsylvania, Births and Christenings, 1709-1950 collection is name-searchable and holds christening entries that would give a birth or baptism date and the parents' names. Search by her name with the 1893-1905 window, then check the parents against Patrick Flynn; the mother is not yet named in the tree.

Fallback if the christening index has no entry for Margaret. The Pennsylvania, Delayed Birth Records, 1780-1977 collection is name-searchable and holds late-filed registrations of births never recorded at the time, a common case for an anthracite-region family around 1897. A delayed record would state a birth date and place under oath.

The United States, Census, 1900 collection is name-searchable and should show Margaret, about three, in her parents' household. Her age, month and year of birth, and Pennsylvania birthplace are a derivative check on the 1897 estimate, not proof of the exact date. The enumerator's entries also give the parents' birthplaces and the household's address, which identifies the parish to search in item 5.

The Schuylkill County Orphans' Court kept registers of births and deaths for 1893-1905, which covers Margaret's estimated birth. The locality entry does not say whether these registers are indexed or open to request (access unknown), so this item is a request or browse at the court, not a name search. Fallback for the christening and delayed-birth items if neither names her.

Margaret's baptism, if she was Catholic, is held in the sacramental register of her parish, not at the county. Schuylkill stayed under the Archdiocese of Philadelphia until 1961, so the Philadelphia archdiocesan archive is a second route. The browse-only church register volume in Schuylkill ends in 1895 and does not reach a 1897 baptism, so this needs the parish register itself. The parish is not yet known; take it from the 1900 census address (item 3). Fallback if the indexed items miss her.

Patrick Flynn died 12 March 1908 in Schuylkill County (tree death fact). Margaret would be about eleven, so a probate file for his estate could name her as a minor heir with an age or a guardian, and the guardian and appraisers are FAN names. The Register of Wills collection is browse-only, so this is an image browse of the 1908 estate dockets, not a name search. Its window is set by the 1908 death, not by Margaret's birth.

Margaret's own death or burial entry, dated after her estimated birth. Death and burial entries often state an age and birthplace, which is the usual route to a birth date when a baptism cannot be found (the tree gives no death date for her). The Pennsylvania, Deaths and Burials, 1720-1999 and Pennsylvania, Cemetery Records collections are name-searchable.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

entry.rationale: The tree's death fact for Patrick (12 Mar 1908, Schuylkill County) cites a Pennsylvania death certificate (S3), but the certificate has not been read for the parents' names. Statewide registration began in 1906, so a 1908 death has a state certificate, which often names the father and mother. The 1850 search (log_001) extracted only Patrick and Thomas Flynn from dwelling 84. The rest of that household, including Thomas's wife and any siblings, was not extracted. The 1850 United States census is name-searchable, but this household needs the image read.

The tree already cites the 1860 census (S2) for the parent-child link, but no 1860 assertion has been extracted and no 1860 search is logged. The 1860 census records each member's relationship to the head, which the 1850 census does not, so it can test whether Patrick is recorded as Thomas's son. Thomas's household in 1870 and 1880 should show whether Patrick and the mother are still with him and whether Patrick is recorded as a son. The 1880 census also gives the birthplace of each person's father and mother, which bears on the Irish origin of the family. Both United States censuses are name-searchable.
