entry.rationale: Log_001 found Patrick Flynn (age 5) in dwelling 84 of Thomas Flynn's household, but the extracted assertions record neither the wife's given name nor the other household members. Re-read the full dwelling image and the adjoining dwellings to obtain the wife's given name, any siblings, and neighbours who are FAN candidates. The 1850 census is name-searchable and does not state relationships, so this item tests composition only; it gives the search for the parents' marriage its given name.

The tree's ParentChild relationship between Thomas Flynn (I2) and Patrick (I1) cites the 1860 U.S. census (S2), but no assertion from the 1860 census exists in research.json, so the cited record has not been read for this question. The 1860 census is name-searchable and, unlike 1850, records each person's relationship to the head of household; a 'son' entry for Patrick in Thomas's household would be direct, not inferred, evidence of parentage.

The 1880 U.S. census is name-searchable and records relationship to the head and each person's parents' birthplaces. Patrick would be about 35. Whether he is a son in Thomas's household (if Thomas survived to 1880) or the head of his own household, the entry tests the parentage claim and may name a household member who is the wife. Ireland-born parents on both sides would be consistent with the tree's Irish birthplace for Patrick, but the parents' birthplace alone does not name them.

The tree's death fact for Patrick (1908-03-12, Schuylkill County) cites the Pennsylvania death certificate (S3), but no parent names are recorded from it. State certificates from 1906 onward name the decedent's father and mother, so the certificate may name Thomas Flynn and the mother's maiden name. The certificate is name-searchable through the Pennsylvania Deaths and Burials collection, with the original held by the state. The informant may be a child or spouse, so the parent names are informant-reported and need corroboration.

Tests whether Patrick was christened in Pennsylvania after the family emigrated; the tree gives Ireland as his birthplace, so a Pennsylvania entry would be a christening after arrival rather than his birth baptism. The Pennsylvania Births and Christenings collection is name-searchable. Catholic sacramental registers are held by the parish or the Diocese of Philadelphia, not the county, so indexed coverage may be partial and a browse of the parish register may be needed if the index is silent.

FAN item: siblings' christenings in Schuylkill County naming Thomas Flynn and the wife as parents would confirm the family unit and identify other children. Each sibling entry names the same parents, so a match to Thomas and a wife with a given name from the 1850 re-read supports the parentage link without relying on Patrick's own record. The Pennsylvania Births and Christenings collection is name-searchable; the search is keyed on the father's name since the mother's name is unknown.

Dedicated item for the candidate parents' marriage to each other, dated before Patrick's birth window closes. The marriage supplies the mother's maiden name only if it was her first marriage, so it does not settle the mother's name on its own; the 1850 re-read supplies her given name to key the search. Church Marriages, Civil Marriages and County Marriages are each name-searchable. If the marriage took place in Ireland it is outside this plan (see the Ireland gap noted for this question). Her other marriages are a separate check (items on mortality and probate).

Pennsylvania Mortality Schedules (1850-1880) are name-searchable and list each person who died in the year before the census, with age, sex and birthplace. If the mother died in that span, the entry gives her age and birthplace, which tests whether the wife named in the 1850 household is the mother and sets her death date. The national mortality schedule is name-searchable for the same years.

Pennsylvania Cemetery Records (ca. 1700-1950) are name-searchable. A burial for Thomas Flynn or the wife may give birth or death dates and ages that bracket the parents' lives, and a shared plot may hold children, which is FAN evidence for siblings. Cemetery entries are secondary, so each lead needs a primary record to confirm it.

The Schuylkill County Register of Wills holds wills and administrations from 1811. Its probate collection is browse-only, so this is an image browse of the Flynn entries, not a name search. The window is sized to Thomas Flynn's plausible lifespan (born about 1818, so a death or will from about 1850 to 1895 falls inside it). A will or administration naming Patrick as a son or heir would be direct parentage evidence, and it may name the wife.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

items.question: Who were the parents of Patrick Flynn (b. ~1845, PA, d. 1908)?
items.rationale: This is the primary research objective.

entry.rationale: The 1850 and 1860 censuses place Patrick in Thomas Flynn's household only by position and surname, so parentage there is indirect. The 1880 census is the first to state each member's relationship to the head of household, and it is a name-searchable United States census collection. It can settle whether Patrick is recorded as Thomas's son.

Patrick was alive in 1900 (he died in 1908), so the 1900 census should show him with a stated relationship to his head of household. This is a second, independent test of parentage. The census is name-searchable, and it may also show whether Thomas was still living in the household.

The 1870 census is the missing link between the 1860 and 1880 enumerations. It can confirm continuity of the Thomas Flynn household and show Patrick's age and birthplace at about 25. The census is name-searchable. Its entries do not state relationships, so this item adds continuity rather than direct parentage.

If Thomas Flynn (born about 1818 in Ireland) died between 1850 and 1880, the US mortality schedules for those years would list him by household. They can give his age, birthplace and cause of death. A household entry linking him to Patrick would help. The national mortality schedule collection is name-searchable.

Dedicated parents' marriage item. Thomas Flynn's marriage to Patrick's mother would give her maiden name, which the census and death certificate do not supply. Its date relative to Patrick's birth (about 1845) would corroborate Thomas as father. It does not by itself prove Patrick is their child. The mother's identity is not yet known, so the search is by Thomas Flynn as groom, across every marriage he may have had in the window. The county marriage collection is name-searchable.

Companion to the marriage item above. Catholic marriages in the anthracite region are recorded in church registers, which the county index may miss. This search tests whether Thomas had an earlier marriage, which would make the wife on the other marriage record not Patrick's mother. It may also give the bride's name and parish. The church marriage collection is name-searchable. Parish registers stay with the Diocese of Philadelphia, not the county, so any hit will need the parish register to be checked.

Thomas Flynn's will or administration file, held by the county Register of Wills from 1811, could name Patrick as a son, which would be direct parentage evidence. The date window follows Thomas's own lifespan (born about 1818), not the research window. The Pennsylvania probate collection is browse-only, so this is an image-by-image browse of the Schuylkill dockets, not a name search.

Burial records for Thomas Flynn and for Patrick (died 1908) may give age, birthplace or the parents' names. The Pennsylvania cemetery collection and the Pennsylvania deaths and burials collection are both name-searchable. This is also a test of the 1908 death certificate's account of Patrick's father.

Thomas Flynn was born in Ireland about 1818, so a declaration of intention or naturalization may name his wife, his residence and his arrival. Those details could corroborate the 1850 household. The Pennsylvania Eastern District naturalization collection is name-searchable. Which federal court handled Schuylkill naturalizations in this period still needs checking against the locality guide. The Middle District collection may need to be searched too.

FAN item. Record the Flynn and related households in the dwellings next to Thomas Flynn's household (dwelling 84 in 1850, dwelling 112 in 1860). Relatives, in-laws and co-migrants from Ireland often lived near each other. A neighbor with the same surname or a shared birthplace could be a sibling, an aunt or uncle, or the source of a name for the mother. The 1850 census is name-searchable, but this search needs the neighbors browsed by dwelling number.

Patrick's own marriage record. Church and county marriage entries often name the groom's parents, which would be a second record naming Thomas. The census shows Patrick had a daughter who married James Brown, so the marriage is likely in this window. The church marriage collection is name-searchable.

The subject's own birth record. The 1850 and 1860 censuses give Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, and Pennsylvania did not begin statewide birth registration until 1906, so no Pennsylvania birth certificate would exist. A baptism in Ireland would need a separate locality survey before it can be planned.
entry.skip_reason: Born in Ireland about 1845 per the 1850 and 1860 censuses. Pennsylvania had no statewide birth registration before 1906.

items.guide_markdown:
## Lincolnshire, England - 1750-1800

FamilySearch's 'England, Births and Christenings' collection (1473014) is a partial Legacy index: it does not index all records for this place or period, and no records or corrections are being added — a nil there is a statement about the index, not proof that no christening exists; search the parish register itself before concluding absence. (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/England,_Births_and_Christenings_-_FamilySearch_Historical_Records)

entry.rationale: Mary Dawson's baptism, about 1772, is the first record that could name her parents. loc_001 lists 'England, Births and Christenings, 1538-1975' (collection 1473014) for this place, but that collection is a partial Legacy index with no additions or corrections, so a nil result does not show that no baptism exists. Search the index for discovery, then verify against the parish register image. The date window allows for a baptism a year either side of the estimated birth.

Full-text search on 'Dawson' with a given name of Mary, unscoped to a collection, to catch a baptism the name index omits or mis-transcribes. The subject's baptism may be indexed under a variant spelling, so the full-text search covers name forms the index misses. Sequenced after item 1 so the index result is known first.

Marriage of the candidate parents. The subject's birth is about 1772, so the couple likely married in the 1750s to early 1770s. The marriage confirms the parents as a couple and, if it was the mother's first marriage, gives her maiden name. No candidate couple exists yet, so the first pass searches Dawson marriages in Lincolnshire in this window to identify one. Where the register names a father, that is a lead to verify, not proof of parentage. Names a couple but does not by itself prove this child is theirs.

Mary Dawson's own marriage, if she married in this window. A marriage record can give her father's name, and a licence or banns entry can give her parish of residence and a witness. It also tests whether 'Dawson' is her birth surname or a later married name, since a remarriage would change which name the marriage record gives. Date window is set by her birth estimate and typical age at marriage.

Mary Dawson's burial or death entry, if it is recorded. Burial entries often state an age and a parish, which can give a birth estimate and a home parish. The baptism may be unreachable if the register is incomplete, so the burial is an independent route to her origin. Window runs from her birth to the latest plausible death. The tree holds no death fact for her.

FAN search on Dawson baptisms, marriages and burials in the same Lincolnshire parishes, targeting siblings and kin who would name the same parents. A sibling's baptism or marriage that names the same parents is direct evidence for Mary's parentage. Also covers bondsmen and witnesses on marriages, who are often the bride's kin. Required on a parentage question.

Wills and administrations of a Dawson parent in Lincolnshire, which may name Mary as a daughter. The window is set by the lifespan of a parent of a child born about 1772: a parent could die anywhere from the child's birth to about 1830. Wills are indexed unevenly, so this item is a browse of the relevant county probate series if no index hit. Repository is the Lincolnshire county archive, which must be confirmed by the researcher.

Fallback to item 1. If the index of 'England, Births and Christenings' gives nothing, browse the Lincolnshire parish register images for baptisms in the estimated window. This is needed because the index is partial and does not show absence. Repository is the parish register holder or Lincolnshire county archive, which the researcher must confirm.

quirks: Records before 1780 are in Elverum prestegjeld — Trysil became its own clerical district in 1780; search Elverum for anything predating that split.

All Trysil church record volumes at FamilySearch are browse-only (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable) — use the indexed national extracts first: Norway Burials 1666–1927 (col 1468081), Norway Baptisms 1634–1927 (col 1467014), Norway Marriages 1660–1926 (col 1468080).
For the 1860 burial, the primary browse volume is 008679203_003 (Trysil church records 1814–1877, 325 images) — must be browsed image by image.

The Trysilboka farm book (Lillevold et al., FS Library 948.23/T2 D2l, multiple volumes) provides farm-level genealogical data for Trysil with personal name indexes in vols 1–3, 7–8 — check for Ziener/Hansen households.

Norwegian conscription/levy rolls (lægdsruller) began 1789 — a male born ~1780 would be enrolled under his father's name from approximately age 9, providing direct parentage evidence; access via Riksarkivet and Digitalarkivet.

Probate volumes at FS Catalog cover Sør-Østerdal only to 1853; for an 1860 estate use the Norway Probate Index Cards (FS col 1661306) to locate the reference, then retrieve the actual volume from Riksarkivet or Digitalarkivet.
Trysil Frimenighet (dissenter congregation) kept separate registers 1858–1920 at Digitalarkivet — check if subject had dissenter affiliation.
All Kongsberg church record volumes at FamilySearch are browse-only (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable); browse image by image for pre-1800 baptisms.

The national indexed extract (Norway Baptisms, col 1467014) has 28,370 Kongsberg records searchable but coverage of the 1780s period may be incomplete; a nil result is a reason to browse, not a conclusion.

Prime FamilySearch volume for a ~1780 baptism is 008680156_003 (church records 1769–1782, 382 images, browse-only); the same register is available at Digitalarkivet under Kongsberg/Kongsberg Parish Church Records 1696–1969.

Kongsberg was an industrial mining town dominated by the Kongsberg Sølvverk (royal silver mine, founded 1624); many residents were miners, and Low German occupational terms pervaded local naming — the alias 'Ziener' may derive from mining terminology.

quirks: Although Mexicans use two surnames, most indexed records carry only the first (paternal) surname — search with the paternal surname alone; when the person is not found, search through the parents (a parent search with each parent's first surname, leaving out the child's name). (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Norway_Church_Records)
Before about 1850 most Norwegians used patronymics: Halsteinsdatter means daughter of Halstein. (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Norway_Naming_Customs)

Meland, including the farm Hestdal, was a sokn (annex parish) of Hamre prestegjeld; its baptisms, marriages and burials are in the Hamre kirkebøker, 1677-1928. (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Meland_Parish,_Hordaland,_Norway_Genealogy)

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1845-1908

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Probate is held by the county Register of Wills from 1811. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906, so pre-1906 vital events depend on church, cemetery, and probate records. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only.

Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1840-1900

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906 -- pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only. Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.
